frames.narration: A payments service on host h-417 hits a timeout and writes one JSON line to its log file: level error, service payments, tenant acme, message card gateway timeout. Writing to a file is cheap, and the service does not wait for the log platform at all.
The agent tails the file. It gathers lines until it has 1,000 or 5 seconds have passed, compresses the 300 kB batch to about 38 kB and sends it, with a batch id, to the ingest gateway.

The gateway checks the tenant. Acme is using 3.1 MB/s of its 20 MB/s limit, so the batch is accepted, and the gateway appends it to the replicated queue. Only when the queue acknowledges does the agent move its saved offset to 48,210.

A parser takes the batch from the queue at its own pace. It reads the JSON, adds host h-417 and region eu-west, masks a card number that someone had put in a message, and drops the batch id if it had been seen before.

The parser writes the lines in two places. The compressed lines go into a chunk in object storage, and a small entry goes into the label index: service payments, level error, tenant acme, and the time range of the chunk. The index holds no words from the message.

Within about 10 seconds of the service writing the line (up to 5 of them waiting for the batch to fill), it is searchable. An engineer who is paged opens the log search and asks for level error, service payments, the words card gateway, in the last 15 minutes.

The query service asks the label index which chunks match the labels and the time range. The 15 minutes hold 540 chunks written by all services, and the index names 12 of them. The other 528 are never touched.

The query workers read those 12 chunks in parallel from object storage and scan them for the words. 37 lines match and come back newest first, with the first page shown at once. The time range kept the search to the hot tier, and a search of last month would have read the same way, just from the warm one.
